title: Normalization (1NF to BCNF) and when to denormalize
scopeHtml: Scope: update/insert/delete anomalies, functional dependencies, 1NF to BCNF, and safe denormalization techniques.

notes.title: Why normalization exists: anomalies
notes.html:
Normalization is organising tables so each fact is stored exactly once. If a fact lives in many places, they drift apart, and you get three classic bugs called anomalies.

Imagine one big table orders_flat(order_id, customer_name, customer_city, product, price):

  • Update anomaly: a customer moves city; you must update 400 rows; miss one and the data contradicts itself.
  • Insert anomaly: you can't record a new customer until they place an order.
  • Delete anomaly: deleting the customer's only order also erases the fact that the customer exists.

Worked example. 1M orders from 50k customers. In the flat table the city string repeats 20 times per customer on average: 1M x ~12 bytes = 12 MB of redundant city text, and one move means touching ~20 rows. Normalised: 50k city values, one row update.

Industry examples. Core OLTP systems (banking ledgers, Stripe's customer/charge tables, Shopify orders) are normalised because correctness beats a few extra joins. Analytics warehouses (BigQuery, Redshift) deliberately denormalise, which is the next-to-last section.

Everyday analogy. Writing your phone number on 30 sticky notes. When it changes, you will forget one note.

Common interview traps.

  • Defining normalization as "splitting tables". The goal is one fact in one place.
  • Not being able to name the three anomalies with an example.

notes.title: Functional dependencies (the tool behind everything)
notes.html:
A functional dependency A -> B means: if two rows have the same A, they must have the same B. customer_id -> customer_city holds because a customer lives in one city. order_id, product_id -> qty holds in an order-lines table.

A candidate key is a minimal set of columns that determines every other column. Normal forms are rules about which dependencies are allowed relative to the keys.

orders_flat(order_id, product_id, customer_id, customer_city, product_name, qty)
Key: (order_id, product_id)
  order_id               -> customer_id          (part of key only: partial dependency)
  customer_id            -> customer_city        (non-key determines non-key: transitive)
  product_id             -> product_name         (part of key only)
  order_id, product_id   -> qty                  (full key: fine)

Vocabulary: prime attribute = part of some candidate key. Non-prime = not part of any key. Partial dependency = non-prime depends on part of a composite key. Transitive dependency = key -> X -> Y where X is not a key.

Worked example. In the table above, order_id -> customer_id means every order line repeats the customer. If an order has 10 lines, customer_id is stored 10 times; changing the customer on an order means 10 writes and a chance of 9.

Everyday analogy. A postcode determines the city. If your address book stores both, the city is redundant given the postcode.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up the direction: A -> B does not imply B -> A.
  • Forgetting to first identify the key before judging a normal form.

notes.title: 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups
notes.html:
First normal form: every column holds a single indivisible value, every row is unique, and there are no repeating column groups.

Violations:

  • A column storing 'red,green,blue' or a JSON array you query inside.
  • Repeating columns: phone1, phone2, phone3.
  • No key at all, so duplicate rows can exist.
-- Bad: list in a column
CREATE TABLE student_bad (id int PRIMARY KEY, name text, courses text); -- 'math,physics'

-- 1NF: one row per fact
CREATE TABLE enrolment (
  student_id int, course text,
  PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course)
);
-- Now this is a plain index lookup instead of LIKE '%physics%' (full scan)
SELECT student_id FROM enrolment WHERE course = 'physics';

Worked example. Finding students of physics with LIKE '%physics%' over 2M rows needs a seq scan, about 100 to 400 ms. After 1NF with an index on course, it is under 1 ms plus the rows returned. Also 'physics' vs 'astrophysics' stops matching by accident.

Grey zone. Postgres arrays and jsonb technically break the strict rule, yet are fine when you treat the value as opaque or index it with GIN and never need joins or per-element constraints. Be able to say that nuance.

Industry examples. Early MySQL apps with CSV-in-a-column tags were a common migration pain; tag systems (GitHub labels, Stack Overflow tags) use a junction table.

Everyday analogy. One item per line on a shopping list rather than "milk, eggs, bread" all on one line, so you can tick items off one at a time.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying arrays/jsonb always violate 1NF. It is about how you use them.
  • Forgetting that a table with no PK can hold duplicates.

notes.title: 2NF: no partial dependencies
notes.html:
Second normal form: be in 1NF, and every non-key column depends on the WHOLE key, not just part of it. This only matters when the key is composite.

Table order_line(order_id, product_id, qty, product_name) with key (order_id, product_id). product_name depends on product_id alone: partial dependency.

-- Split product facts out
CREATE TABLE product (product_id int PRIMARY KEY, product_name text NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE order_line (
  order_id int, product_id int REFERENCES product,
  qty int NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)
);

Worked example. 20M order lines, product_name averaging 30 bytes: 600 MB of repeated names. After 2NF, 100k products x 30 B = 3 MB, and renaming a product is one row.

Careful. Snapshot columns (price at the time of sale) look like partial dependencies but are deliberate: the price at purchase time is a fact about the order line, not about the product today.

If the key is a single column, a table in 1NF is automatically in 2NF.

Industry examples. Every order system keeps a product table and references it; Shopify copies title and price into line_items as a snapshot on purpose.

Everyday analogy. A receipt shows quantity per product; it should not retell each product's whole description every line.

Common interview traps.

  • Claiming snapshot columns violate 2NF. They record a historical fact.
  • Applying 2NF to single-column-key tables (always satisfied).

notes.title: 3NF: no transitive dependencies
notes.html:
Third normal form: be in 2NF, and no non-key column depends on another non-key column. "Every non-key column depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key."

employee(emp_id PK, dept_id, dept_name): emp_id -> dept_id -> dept_name. dept_name depends on dept_id, not directly on the key.

CREATE TABLE department (dept_id int PRIMARY KEY, dept_name text NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE employee (
  emp_id  int PRIMARY KEY,
  dept_id int NOT NULL REFERENCES department
);

Worked example. Renaming "Engineering" to "Platform" in the flat table touches all 8,000 engineers (and risks inconsistency, "Engineering" and "Platform" both existing). In 3NF it is one row update.

Formal 3NF (for interviews). For each dependency X -> A, either X is a superkey, or A is part of some candidate key. The second clause is what BCNF removes.

Industry examples. Most ORM-modelled business apps are 3NF by default. Reference data (countries, currencies, statuses) lives in lookup tables.

Decision gravity. Normalising is reversible (you can denormalise later with a view or copy), and splitting a table in production is a migration, not a catastrophe. Over-normalising a hot read path is the more common regret, handled in the last section.

Everyday analogy. A student card shows the school ID, not the school's full address; the address lives in one school record.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying 3NF means "no redundancy at all". Some remains (keys repeat as FKs).
  • Not knowing the "key, whole key, nothing but the key" summary.

notes.title: BCNF: every determinant is a key
notes.html:
Boyce-Codd normal form: for every dependency X -> Y, X must be a superkey. It is a stricter 3NF that closes a loophole when a table has overlapping candidate keys.

Example: class_slot(student, subject, teacher). Rules: each teacher teaches ONE subject; a student has one teacher per subject. Keys: (student, subject) and (student, teacher). Dependency teacher -> subject exists, but teacher is not a key. This is in 3NF (subject is part of a key) but violates BCNF: teacher "Rao -> Maths" is repeated for every student.

CREATE TABLE teacher_subject (teacher text PRIMARY KEY, subject text NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE student_teacher (
  student text, teacher text REFERENCES teacher_subject,
  PRIMARY KEY (student, teacher)
);

Trade-off. BCNF decomposition may lose the ability to enforce the rule "a student has one teacher per subject" with a plain key constraint (you can't express (student, subject) uniqueness across the split without a trigger or extra join). That is why some designs stay at 3NF. 3NF is always lossless and dependency preserving; BCNF is lossless but not always dependency preserving.

Worked example. 100k students x 6 subjects = 600k rows. Before: Rao's subject repeated 600k/200 teachers = 3,000 times each. After: 200 rows in teacher_subject.

Higher forms, one line each. 4NF removes independent multi-valued facts stored together (a person's hobbies and languages in one table, causing a cross product). 5NF removes join dependencies. 6NF is temporal (one fact per row over time). Interviews rarely go past BCNF/4NF.

Everyday analogy. A timetable listing "teacher Rao, subject Maths" on every student line, instead of one board saying Rao teaches Maths.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing 3NF and BCNF are the same. They differ with overlapping candidate keys.
  • Saying BCNF is always better; dependency preservation can be lost.

notes.title: When to denormalize
notes.html:
Denormalization is deliberately storing the same fact in more than one place to make reads cheaper. You pay with write complexity and risk of drift. Normalise first; denormalise with a measurement in hand.

Common techniques:

  • Copy a column (store author_name in posts).
  • Precomputed counters (comment_count on posts) so you avoid COUNT(*) over millions of rows.
  • Summary / rollup tables (daily revenue per shop) refreshed by jobs.
  • Materialized views (Postgres CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW, refresh manually or on schedule).
  • jsonb snapshot of a related object.
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW daily_revenue AS
  SELECT date_trunc('day', created_at) AS d, shop_id, sum(total_cents) AS cents
  FROM orders GROUP BY 1, 2;
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON daily_revenue (d, shop_id);
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY daily_revenue;  -- needs the unique index

Worked example. Feed page needs author name for 20 posts. Join cost: 20 index lookups, about 1 ms total, so DON'T denormalise this. But SELECT count(*) FROM likes WHERE post_id = X on a 10-billion-row table with a celebrity post of 50M likes costs seconds; a stored like_count makes it O(1), updated by a queue or sharded counters (hot row contention becomes the new problem: 50k increments/s on one row serialises on its lock).

Industry examples. Instagram and Twitter store like/follower counts as counters, accepting slight lag. Data warehouses use star schemas (fact table plus denormalised dimensions) to cut joins for analytics. Stack Overflow keeps Score/AnswerCount columns on Posts.

Decision gravity. Adding a derived column is easy and reversible; keeping it correct for years is the real cost. Prefer: constraint or trigger or one write path; add a periodic reconcile job that recomputes and alerts on drift.

Production incident pattern. Counter drifts after a retry double-counts. Symptom: user sees "3 comments" but lists 2. Metric: reconcile job's mismatch count rises. Fix: make updates idempotent (derive from events) or recompute.

Everyday analogy. Keeping a running total on the cashier's screen instead of re-adding the whole receipt each time. Fast, but if you forget to update it, it lies.

Common interview traps.

  • Denormalising on day one without measuring; first fix indexes and queries.
  • Not saying how you keep the copy consistent.
  • Ignoring hot-row contention on a shared counter.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Normalization = one fact in one place; it prevents update, insert and delete anomalies.
  • Functional dependency A -> B is the tool; find the key first.
  • 1NF atomic values; 2NF no partial dependency on a composite key; 3NF no transitive dependency ("key, whole key, nothing but the key"); BCNF every determinant is a superkey.
  • 3NF is always lossless and dependency preserving; BCNF may lose dependency preservation.
  • Snapshots (price at sale) are deliberate, not violations.
  • Denormalise only with measurements: counters, rollups, materialized views, copied columns; plan a reconcile job.
  • Normalise first (reversible, cheap); denormalising a hot path later is safer than guessing early.

questions.promptHtml: What problem does normalization solve? Explain update, insert and delete anomalies with an example.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you can state the purpose, not just recite normal forms.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Normalization removes redundancy so each fact is stored once. Redundant copies cause anomalies. Update: change a customer's city in one row but not the other 40 rows. Insert: you cannot record a new product until someone orders it. Delete: removing the last order erases the only record of the customer."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Flat table order_flat(order_id, customer_id, customer_city, product, price):

order_id | customer_id | customer_city | product | price
   1     |     7       |  Pune         | pen     | 10
   2     |     7       |  Pune         | bag     | 700
   3     |     7       |  Delhi        | pen     | 10     <- inconsistent copy
  • Update anomaly: city lives in every order row, so a move needs N updates, and a partial failure leaves contradictions.
  • Insert anomaly: a customer with no orders has no row (or needs NULL product).
  • Delete anomaly: deleting order 3 may delete the only record of that customer's city. The fix is to put each fact in the table whose key determines it: customer(id, city), product(id, price), order_item(order_id, product_id).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
-- check for contradictions caused by redundancy
SELECT customer_id FROM order_flat GROUP BY customer_id HAVING count(DISTINCT customer_city) > 1;

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying normalization is "about saving disk". It is mainly about correctness.
  • Thinking more tables is always better.
  • Confusing normalization with indexing.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a foreign key fix redundancy? -> No; it only checks existence, not duplicated attributes.
  2. Can a NULL-heavy table be an anomaly sign? -> Yes, mixed facts in one row.
  3. Why do warehouses accept redundancy? -> Append-only loads and read speed; no concurrent updates to correct.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer lists three anomalies. The senior ties each to a concrete failure and says normalization is about a single source of truth.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Customer address copied onto every invoice produced a dispute when two invoices for the same customer showed different cities.

questions.promptHtml: What does First Normal Form require, and is storing a JSON column or an array a violation?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Common confusion between theory and Postgres practice.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "1NF means each column holds a single atomic value, there are no repeating column groups like phone1, phone2, phone3, and each row is uniquely identifiable. A comma-separated list violates it. A JSON or array column is a grey area: it is fine when the value is treated as an opaque document and never filtered, joined or constrained by its parts."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
"Atomic" means the database never needs to look inside the value. Violations:

user(id, phones)         -> '9811,9822,9833'      (list in one cell)
user(id, phone1, phone2) -> repeating group

Why it hurts: WHERE phones LIKE '%9822%' cannot use a B-tree and matches '19822'; no FK or UNIQUE per phone; no per-phone metadata. Fix with a child table user_phone(user_id, phone, kind) with PK (user_id, phone). JSONB/arrays with GIN indexes can be queried well, so they are pragmatic for sparse, rarely-joined data; but you lose FKs and per-element constraints.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
CREATE TABLE user_phone (
  user_id bigint REFERENCES users(id),
  phone   text NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (user_id, phone)
);

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking JSON automatically violates 1NF, or that it never does.
  • Splitting a name into 3 columns "for 1NF" when it is a single logical value for your use.
  • Forgetting 1NF also requires a key.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is a date atomic? -> Yes for most uses; "atomic" depends on the operations you need.
  2. Tags as array vs join table? -> Join table if you need counts, FKs or tag metadata; array+GIN for simple containment.
  3. Why does UNIQUE on a list column fail? -> It only compares the whole string.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "no multi-valued columns". The senior frames atomic relative to access patterns and knows when jsonb is the right call.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Role lists stored as 'admin,editor' caused a LIKE-based permission check to grant 'superadmin' users to 'admin' queries.

questions.promptHtml: What is a functional dependency, and how do you use it to find the candidate keys of a table?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Foundation for 2NF to BCNF reasoning; classic whiteboard exercise.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "X -> Y means that whenever two rows agree on X they must agree on Y, so X determines Y. To find keys, I compute the attribute closure of a column set: keep adding everything determined by what I already have. A set whose closure covers all columns, and is minimal, is a candidate key."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Example R(A,B,C,D) with FDs: A -> B, B -> C, C D -> A.

  • Closure of {A}: A -> B, B -> C, so {A,B,C}; D is missing, so A is not a key.
  • Closure of {A,D}: {A,B,C,D}, a candidate key (neither A nor D alone works).
  • Closure of {C,D}: gets A, then B: all, also a key. Another candidate: {B,D} (B->C, then CD->A). FDs are facts about the business rule (a zip code determines city), not about the current data; data can only disprove an FD.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
-- test whether city -> state holds in current data (can only refute)
SELECT city FROM places GROUP BY city HAVING count(DISTINCT state) > 1;

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Inferring an FD from a sample of data.
  • Forgetting that composite determinants need all columns.
  • Missing candidate keys by stopping after the first.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What are Armstrong's axioms? -> Reflexivity, augmentation, transitivity.
  2. Trivial FD? -> Y subset of X.
  3. Minimal cover? -> Remove extraneous attributes and redundant FDs; used to derive 3NF.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer defines the arrow. The senior computes closures quickly and says FDs come from business rules, not data.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A schema assumed zip -> city, which failed for shared zips and corrupted shipping labels.

questions.contextHtml:
A support dashboard shows revenue by customer tier. Numbers do not add up: total by tier is 4% higher than total orders. Table:

CREATE TABLE order_lines (
  order_id bigint, line_no int, customer_id bigint, customer_tier text,
  product_id bigint, product_name text, unit_price int, qty int,
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, line_no));
-- illustrative query
SELECT customer_tier, sum(unit_price*qty) FROM order_lines GROUP BY 1;
SELECT customer_id, count(DISTINCT customer_tier) FROM order_lines GROUP BY 1 HAVING count(DISTINCT customer_tier) > 1;  -- 1,812 customers

Tier changes via a nightly job that updates only the last 30 days of rows. Red herring: a recent timezone fix.
questions.promptHtml: Why is the report wrong and how do you fix the design?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Fixes the job to update all rows. This leaves the root cause.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Should revenue be attributed to the tier at order time or current tier? Who owns tier? How many rows (volume)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Report from a join to the authoritative customer table so numbers reconcile today.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Redundant customer_tier on every line drifted (update anomaly); duplicates from the join; timezone cutoff. The HAVING query already shows 1,812 customers with 2+ tiers.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare sum(unit_price*qty) to the orders total; run the distinct-tier query; check job SQL.
  5. Root cause: customer_id -> customer_tier is a dependency outside the key (order_id, line_no): customer data stored per line. Changing it in part of the rows leaves contradictory copies. The 4% is the double counting when one customer appears under two tiers in a rollup that the report later joined on.
  6. Fix: Move tier to customers(id, tier). If the business wants "tier at time of order", that is a new fact: store tier_at_order on orders deliberately, set once, never updated.
ALTER TABLE order_lines DROP COLUMN customer_tier;
SELECT c.tier, sum(l.unit_price*l.qty) FROM order_lines l
JOIN orders o USING (order_id) JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id GROUP BY 1;
  1. Prevention: Design review rule: every non-key column must depend on the whole key and nothing but it.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not "fix the job" and keep the redundancy; not delete rows. Migration: backfill from customers, verify, then drop the column.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• 5B rows, cannot drop quickly? -> Create the view first, stop writes to the column, drop in a low-traffic window or via new table.
  • Need tier history? -> customer_tier_history(customer_id, tier, valid_from, valid_to).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A finance report disagreed with billing by 3% because a nightly job updated only recent rows of a denormalised column.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Patches the job.
  • Hire: Identifies redundancy and moves the attribute.
  • Strong hire: Distinguishes current vs at-order tier and plans the migration.

questions.promptHtml: Explain 2NF and 3NF with one example each, and the difference in what they remove.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The standard question; the nuance is in the "partial" vs "transitive" distinction.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "2NF applies to composite keys: every non-key column must depend on the whole key, not part of it. 3NF says non-key columns must depend only on the key, not on another non-key column. Partial dependency is a piece of the key determining something; transitive is key -> A -> B."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
2NF violation: order_item(order_id, product_id, qty, product_name): product_id -> product_name depends on half the key. Fix: move name to product. 3NF violation: employee(id, dept_id, dept_name): id -> dept_id -> dept_name, dept_name depends on a non-key. Fix: department(id, name).

2NF: key = (A,B), A -> C   => split C out with A
3NF: key = K,  K -> X -> Y => split Y out with X

A one-line memory aid: "the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key". Tables with a single-column key automatically satisfy 2NF.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
CREATE TABLE department (id int PRIMARY KEY, name text NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE employee (id int PRIMARY KEY, dept_id int NOT NULL REFERENCES department(id));

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Applying 2NF reasoning to a table with a surrogate single-column PK and concluding it is "fine", while ignoring natural-key dependencies.
  • Mixing up partial and transitive.
  • Normalizing without asking about actual FDs.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is a table with PK id and zip -> city in 3NF? -> No, zip -> city is transitive.
  2. Why do prime attributes get special treatment in 3NF? -> 3NF allows Y if Y is part of a candidate key; BCNF does not.
  3. Does 3NF always preserve dependencies? -> Yes, a lossless and dependency-preserving 3NF decomposition always exists.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer recites the mantra. The senior points out surrogate keys can hide 2NF issues and that you verify against natural keys.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Product names stored in line items caused a rename to require updating 90M rows and a long table lock.

questions.contextHtml:
An articles table keeps tags text as 'sql,postgres,index'. 4M articles. Queries: "articles tagged postgres" via WHERE tags LIKE '%postgres%' takes 2.4 s (seq scan, illustrative):

-- illustrative
Seq Scan on articles  (actual time=0.1..2380 rows=18400)
  Filter: (tags ~~ '%postgres%'::text)   Rows Removed by Filter: 3981600

It also returns articles tagged 'postgresql' and 'postgres-xl'. The tag list page needs counts per tag, done by splitting strings in the app. Editors want to rename a tag.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do and what are the options?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add a trigram index" fixes speed only; leaves wrong matches, no counts or rename.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are tags a controlled vocabulary? Average tags per article (3-5)? Is tag metadata needed (slug, description)? Read vs write ratio?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Use string_to_array with = ANY for exact match, or add a GIN index on string_to_array(tags, ',') to stop wrong matches and the scan.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: N/A for diagnosis: list-in-a-cell is a 1NF violation. Options: join table, array column with GIN, jsonb.
  4. How I'd verify each: Prototype with 4M rows and compare plans for tag lookup and tag counts.
  5. Root cause: Multi-valued attribute stored non-atomically; the database cannot index, constrain or count by element.
  6. Fix: Many-to-many tables:
CREATE TABLE tag (id int PRIMARY KEY, slug text UNIQUE NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE article_tag (article_id bigint REFERENCES articles, tag_id int REFERENCES tag,
                          PRIMARY KEY (article_id, tag_id));
CREATE INDEX ON article_tag (tag_id, article_id);
-- illustrative after: Index Only Scan using article_tag_tag_id_article_id_idx (actual time=0.03..4.1 rows=18400)

Backfill with unnest(string_to_array(tags, ',')) in batches. 7. Prevention: Review rule: no delimited lists in a column. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Arrays+GIN is simpler if tags are never renamed or counted by metadata; I'd choose the join table because renames and counts matter. Not a trigram index as the primary fix.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• 200M articles? -> Partition article_tag by hash of article_id or tag popularity; cache tag counts.
  • Free-text tags with typos? -> Normalise to lowercase slug at write time.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A CMS search for tag 'sql' matched 'mysql', 'nosql' and silently polluted a newsletter segment.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Adds an index and moves on.
  • Hire: Moves to a join table or array+GIN with reasons.
  • Strong hire: Compares options, backfills in batches, plans for renames and counts.

questions.promptHtml: What is BCNF and when is a table in 3NF but not in BCNF? Give an example.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who know the edge case of overlapping candidate keys.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "BCNF requires that for every non-trivial FD X -> Y, X is a superkey. 3NF is weaker: it also allows Y to be part of a candidate key. A table can be in 3NF but not BCNF when a non-key column determines part of a candidate key, usually with overlapping composite candidate keys."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Classic: teaches(student, course, instructor) with rules: a student has one instructor per course (student, course) -> instructor, and each instructor teaches only one course instructor -> course.

  • Candidate keys: (student, course) and (student, instructor).
  • instructor -> course: course is a prime attribute so 3NF accepts it, but instructor is not a superkey, so BCNF is violated.
  • Anomaly: if instructor X switches courses, every student row must be updated; the fact "X teaches DB" cannot be stored without a student. Decomposition: (instructor, course) and (student, instructor). Cost: the FD (student, course) -> instructor can no longer be checked by one table's key, so you can no longer enforce "one instructor per student per course" with a simple constraint.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
CREATE TABLE instructor_course (instructor_id int PRIMARY KEY, course_id int NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE student_instructor (student_id int, instructor_id int REFERENCES instructor_course,
                                 PRIMARY KEY (student_id, instructor_id));

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Claiming BCNF is always better than 3NF.
  • Not knowing BCNF may lose dependency preservation.
  • Missing the second candidate key.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is BCNF decomposition lossless? -> Yes always, but may not preserve all FDs.
  2. Which would you ship? -> Often 3NF plus a trigger/constraint for the lost FD; or BCNF plus an assertion-like check.
  3. Do real schemas hit this? -> Rare, mostly with overlapping composite keys.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "stricter 3NF". The senior shows the example, the lost-FD cost and states when to stop at 3NF.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A scheduling table with overlapping keys had 7% inconsistent room-teacher pairs after a manual data fix.

questions.contextHtml: Finance exports a monthly CSV that the team must load into Postgres: invoice_no, invoice_date, customer_code, customer_name, customer_address, line_no, sku, sku_description, unit_price, qty, tax_rate. About 2M rows per month. A junior loaded it as one table with PK (invoice_no, line_no). Now product asks for "an invoice screen and a customer page". The interviewer adds nothing else.
questions.promptHtml: How do you design the tables? What do you ask first?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Keeps one table "because it matches the file", or splits into 10 tables without checking dependencies.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can unit_price differ from the catalog price (discounts, history)? Is tax per line or per invoice? Can customer name change and should old invoices show the old name? Is customer_code stable?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Load raw CSV into a staging table untouched, then transform; never fix inside the raw load.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Dependencies I'd test: invoice_no -> invoice_date, customer_code (partial: half the key), customer_code -> name, address, sku -> sku_description. unit_price and tax_rate I treat as per-line facts until proven otherwise.
  4. How I'd verify each: For each suspected FD, GROUP BY lhs HAVING count(DISTINCT rhs) > 1 over a month of data; any hit means the FD does not hold.
  5. Root cause: In the flat file, invoice and customer facts repeat on every line: 2NF/3NF violations.
  6. Fix:
CREATE TABLE customer (code text PRIMARY KEY, name text NOT NULL, address text);
CREATE TABLE sku (sku text PRIMARY KEY, description text NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE invoice (invoice_no text PRIMARY KEY, invoice_date date NOT NULL,
                      customer_code text NOT NULL REFERENCES customer);
CREATE TABLE invoice_line (invoice_no text REFERENCES invoice, line_no int, sku text REFERENCES sku,
                      unit_price numeric(12,2) NOT NULL, qty int NOT NULL CHECK (qty > 0), tax_rate numeric(5,2) NOT NULL,
                      PRIMARY KEY (invoice_no, line_no));

Load with INSERT ... SELECT DISTINCT ON (...) per table. 7. Prevention: Constraint violations during load reveal FD breaks; reconcile totals between CSV and tables. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: unit_price stays on the line (a historical fact), not looked up from sku. If invoices must show the name as it was, I'd copy it onto the invoice on purpose and document it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Same customer_code with two names in the file? -> The FD fails; ask business, maybe code is not a key.
  • Load speed? -> COPY into staging, then set-based inserts.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A migration trusted customer_code -> name and silently merged two customers that shared a code after a company merger.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: One table or arbitrary splitting.
  • Hire: Identifies FDs and decomposes to 3NF.
  • Strong hire: Tests FDs on data, keeps historical price, handles name drift, and stages the load.

questions.contextHtml:
A social feed page joins 6 tables (posts, users, follows, likes, comments, media). p95 is 1.8 s at 3,000 requests/sec peak; the DB CPU is 85%. The feed is read 200x more than written. Plan excerpt (illustrative):

-- illustrative
Hash Join (actual time=410..1620 rows=50 loops=1)
  -> Aggregate (like counts) (actual time=300..900 rows=1.2M)
  -> Aggregate (comment counts) (actual time=200..700 rows=800k)

Likes can be 5 seconds stale. A teammate wants to "denormalize everything into one wide table"; another says never denormalize.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Either extreme. Or adds a cache with no consistency plan.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Staleness budget per field? Write rate of likes? Does anything else need exact counts (billing, moderation)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cache the hot first page for 5 s with request coalescing.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Per-request aggregates over millions of like/comment rows are the cost; the joins themselves are cheap. Check index usage but the aggregates dominate.
  4. How I'd verify each: EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), pg_stat_statements total time by query.
  5. Root cause: Computing derived values (counts) on every read.
  6. Fix: Keep the normalized tables as the source of truth; add targeted derived data: counters on posts (like_count, comment_count) updated by a worker or trigger, or a materialized view / read table refreshed every few seconds:
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW post_stats AS
SELECT p.id, count(DISTINCT l.user_id) likes, count(DISTINCT c.id) comments
FROM posts p LEFT JOIN likes l ON l.post_id=p.id LEFT JOIN comments c ON c.post_id=p.id GROUP BY p.id;
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ON post_stats (id);
REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY post_stats;

For hot paths use incremental counters instead of full refresh. 7. Prevention: A reconciliation job that recomputes counts nightly and alerts on drift. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a single wide table (update anomalies across 6 entities). Denormalize only derived, tolerance-bound values; keep the source tables authoritative.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Viral post with 50k likes/sec? -> Sharded counters or batch increments; a single row becomes a hot spot.
  • Full refresh takes 40 s? -> Move to incremental maintenance.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A feed cut DB CPU from 85% to 30% with two counter columns; the "wide table" idea would have needed a rewrite on every profile edit.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: All-or-nothing stance.
  • Hire: Adds derived counters or a matview.
  • Strong hire: Uses staleness budgets, keeps source of truth, plans reconciliation and hot-row issues.

questions.promptHtml: When is a decomposition lossless, and how do you show a decomposition that is lossy? Why does it matter in practice?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know splitting tables can create bogus data on re-join.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A decomposition of R into R1 and R2 is lossless if joining them gives exactly R back. The test: the common attributes must be a key of at least one of the parts (R1 ∩ R2 -> R1 or R2). If not, the join produces spurious rows. In practice it explains why you split on a determinant, not on arbitrary columns."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Bad split of works(emp, project, skill) where no FD links them: R1(emp, project) and R2(project, skill). Common column is project, which is not a key of either. Joining returns every employee x every skill on that project, including combinations that never existed.

R1: (Ann, P1) (Bob, P1)   R2: (P1, SQL) (P1, Java)
join: Ann-P1-SQL, Ann-P1-Java, Bob-P1-SQL, Bob-P1-Java   <- 4 rows, source had 2

Good split: on an FD X -> Y, produce (X, Y) and (X, rest). X is the key of the first part, so the join is lossless. Dependency preservation is separate: every FD should be checkable within one table. Lossless is mandatory; preservation is desirable (3NF gives both, BCNF gives only lossless).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
-- detect spurious rows after a split
SELECT count(*) FROM r1 JOIN r2 USING (project);   -- should equal count(*) of original

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Splitting "to reduce width" without a determinant.
  • Treating the join row count as a quick but non-proof test.
  • Believing lossless means no NULLs.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a vertical partition for performance break this? -> Not if both parts keep the full key.
  2. What is a multivalued dependency? -> Independent sets of values per key, handled by 4NF.
  3. How do you verify in a migration? -> Compare counts and checksums of the rejoined set against the original.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer says "no data loss". The senior gives the key-intersection test and the example of spurious tuples.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A reporting split on project multiplied headcount by skills and doubled a payroll estimate.

questions.contextHtml: accounts has 180M rows and 90 columns, including company_name, company_tier, company_billing_country, company_vat_id repeated per account (companies average 40 accounts). Updating a company's tier means updating ~40 rows; a bug left 2.3M accounts with the wrong tier. 6,000 writes/sec, 30k reads/sec, many services read accounts directly via SELECT *. No downtime allowed.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: One big migration script and a deploy at night.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which service owns tier? How many consumers read those columns? Is there a CDC pipeline downstream? Can old and new run together for weeks?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the 2.3M wrong rows by recomputing from the most trusted source in batches.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Risks: lock/rewrite on ALTER, readers breaking on missing columns, dual-write inconsistencies.
  4. How I'd verify each: Staging copy at scale; consumer inventory via pg_stat_statements and code search.
  5. Root cause: company_id -> company_* is a transitive dependency stored on the account row.
  6. Fix: Expand/contract:
  • Create companies; backfill INSERT ... SELECT DISTINCT ON (company_id) in batches.
  • Add accounts.company_id FK as NOT VALID, validate later.
  • Writers dual-write via one service function; a nightly job diffs old vs new columns.
  • Provide a compatibility view accounts_v1 that joins companies and exposes the old columns; move readers to it.
  • After all readers move and diffs are zero for 2 weeks, drop the old columns (DROP COLUMN is metadata-only in Postgres).
CREATE VIEW accounts_v1 AS
SELECT a.*, c.name AS company_name, c.tier AS company_tier FROM accounts a JOIN companies c ON c.id = a.company_id;
  1. Prevention: Ownership doc for each reference attribute; diff job stays as a canary.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not rewrite the whole 180M-row table; not flip readers in one deploy. The view adds a join cost, acceptable with an index on company_id.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Readers use SELECT * and break on column removal? -> View preserves the shape until each is migrated.
  • Backfill saturates IO? -> Throttle batches and watch replica lag.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A rename of a tier code required updating 70M rows twice because two copies existed; after normalization it was a single-row update.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: One-shot migration.
  • Hire: Expand/contract with backfill.
  • Strong hire: Compatibility view, diff canary, FK NOT VALID, and consumer inventory.

questions.contextHtml: The analytics team runs 40 ad hoc queries a day against the OLTP Postgres primary: 7-way joins over orders, items, products, customers, regions; each takes 2 to 8 minutes and one caused replica lag of 90 s last Tuesday. They ask: "Please denormalize the OLTP tables so our queries are simple." OLTP does 2,500 TPS.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Alters the OLTP schema to please analysts, or says "no, use a replica" without more.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Freshness needed (hourly? real time)? Data volume and growth? Which dimensions do they slice by? Existing warehouse?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Move analyst queries to a read replica with hot_standby_feedback considered, plus a statement timeout.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The complaint is query complexity and load, not OLTP correctness. Different workloads want different shapes.
  4. How I'd verify each: pg_stat_statements for time share; replica lag vs analyst queries.
  5. Root cause: One schema serving two access patterns: point writes (normalized) and scans (wide, pre-joined).
  6. Fix: Keep OLTP normalized. Build a separate analytic model: star schema (fact_order_item plus dimension tables) fed by CDC or nightly ETL into a warehouse or a separate Postgres:
CREATE TABLE fact_sales (date_key int, product_key int, customer_key int, region_key int, qty int, amount numeric(12,2));
-- dims hold the descriptive columns, deliberately redundant
  1. Prevention: Query governor and resource limits on replicas; data contracts for the feed.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not denormalize OLTP (writes get slower, anomalies return). Not give analysts the primary. Cost: pipeline and storage, plus data lag.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Need near-real-time? -> CDC stream with incremental materialization.
  • Small data (5 GB)? -> A nightly matview on a replica is enough; don't build a warehouse.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Giving analysts the primary caused a billing slowdown; a nightly star schema removed the issue and cut their queries to 10 s.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Denormalizes OLTP.
  • Hire: Suggests replica or separate store.
  • Strong hire: Star schema, CDC, lag and scale-based choice, governor.

questions.contextHtml: A code reviewer flags: "order_items.unit_price duplicates products.price, this violates 3NF, remove it." The order system has 50M order items. Marketing changes prices weekly; a refund last month for an order from 2023 computed the amount from products.price and refunded $14 too much per unit. Another reviewer says the column is fine.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks a side by rule ("3NF says remove") without asking what the data means.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the item price the price the customer agreed to? Are there discounts or taxes? Legal need to reproduce the invoice?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop the refund job reading products.price; use the item price; recompute wrong refunds.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The two prices are different facts: catalog price (changes over time) vs price charged on this order (immutable).
  4. How I'd verify each: Check whether unit_price ever differs from products.price at order time; look at refund code.
  5. Root cause: The FD product_id -> price does not hold for order items; price depends on (order_id, product_id) and time. It only looks redundant.
  6. Fix: Keep order_items.unit_price (and tax, discount) as a snapshot, write once at checkout, never update, add CHECK (unit_price >= 0). Rename the catalog column to list_price to prevent confusion. Fix the refund code to use the snapshot.
ALTER TABLE products RENAME COLUMN price TO list_price;
SELECT oi.order_id, oi.unit_price, p.list_price FROM order_items oi JOIN products p USING (product_id)
WHERE oi.unit_price <> p.list_price LIMIT 10;
  1. Prevention: Document "snapshot columns" in the schema; tests for refunds after price changes.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not remove the column. Not try to rebuild prices from a price history table unless it is guaranteed complete; a snapshot is simpler and cheaper.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Store price history instead? -> Works with effective dates but joins are harder and error prone; snapshot is the usual answer.
  • Currency change? -> Store currency with the amount.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "cleanup" removed snapshot prices and finance could no longer reproduce a quarter's invoices.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Removes it by rule.
  • Hire: Recognizes snapshot semantics.
  • Strong hire: Fixes the refund bug, renames to avoid confusion, adds checks and tests.

questions.contextHtml: users.follower_count is maintained by the app: UPDATE users SET follower_count = follower_count + 1 after inserting into follows. After a deploy, 3% of users show wrong counts (some negative). Evidence: retries after timeouts re-ran the increment without the insert (the insert was idempotent via ON CONFLICT), and a bulk "remove spam accounts" script deleted follows rows without decrementing. Hot celebrity rows with 4M followers show lock waits of 800 ms.
questions.promptHtml: Review the incident and propose the design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Run a recount script" and stop; or remove the column and count live (4M count per request).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How exact must the count be? Display only or used for logic? Write rate on hot rows?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Recompute from follows in batches and clamp displays at zero.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Two writes in separate steps (not atomic); non-idempotent increment; bypass paths (bulk script); a hot row serialises all follows to one user.
  4. How I'd verify each: SELECT u.id FROM users u WHERE follower_count <> (SELECT count(*) FROM follows WHERE followee_id = u.id) on a sample; lock wait metrics.
  5. Root cause: A derived value kept by hand, with writers that can bypass it.
  6. Fix: Make the update atomic and tied to the row change, in one transaction and only when the insert actually happened:
WITH ins AS (INSERT INTO follows (follower_id, followee_id) VALUES ($1,$2)
             ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING 1)
UPDATE users SET follower_count = follower_count + (SELECT count(*) FROM ins) WHERE id = $2;

Deletes go through the same function, or a trigger. Hot rows: sharded counter table or batched async increments. Add a nightly reconcile job. 7. Prevention: No direct DML on follows except the module; alert when drift > 0.1%. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not live count(*) of 4M rows per request; not trust retries. Eventually consistent counts are fine for display, not for authorization.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Trigger vs app code? -> Trigger covers bypass paths but adds hidden write cost; choose triggers if many writers.
  • Exactness for limits (max 5,000 follows)? -> Enforce with a locked check or a constraint on the authoritative table, not the counter.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "likes" counter drifted 2% a month until a nightly reconciler became part of the contract.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Recount and move on.
  • Hire: Makes increments atomic and idempotent.
  • Strong hire: Handles bypass paths, hot rows, reconciliation and exactness boundaries.
